newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-British inflation slows but disappoints.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-British inflation slows but disappoints.

text.p: Britain's annual inflation rate dipped to 2.1 percent in August but the so-called underlying rate remained stubbornly stuck at 2.8 percent for the fourth month in a row.
The figures disappointed financial markets and economists said they would make it difficult for Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke to justify another pre-election cut in interest rates.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said retail prices rose 0.5 percent month-on-month in August after falling 0.4 percent in July.
"There was upward pressure from a sharp rise in petrol and oil prices," it said. "An upsurge in consumer demand for motor vehicles saw prices rise during the month in contrast to falls last year."
The fall in the overall annual rate was largely due to lower seasonal food prices.
However, underlying annual inflation, which excludes mortgage interest payments, again refused to edge down towards the government target of 2.5 percent or less.
The 2.8 percent annual rate has not changed since May and it is identical to levels seen in June and July last year.
Treasury economic secretary Angela Knight said Britain's long run of sustained low inflation was continuing.
"Britain is now getting the low inflation habit," she said.

But economists said the figures, which followed recent evidence that consumers are spending more and manufacturing is finally emerging from the doldrums, suggested interest rates may have bottomed out.
Clarke has cut rates four times since December to 5.75 percent now.

With an election due by next May and the opposition Labour Party well ahead of the Conservative government in opinion polls, he has a strong political incentive to do what he can to boost the "feel-good factor."

The Bank of England has publicly opposed any further easing in monetary policy and Clarke could face a damaging row with governor Eddie George if he ordered a cut at their next monetary meeting on September 23.
"With the economy strengthening, rate cuts could only be justified by lower inflation -- but inflation has not fallen," said Steve Barrow, an economist at Chase Investment Bank.
Ian Shepherdson, chief UK economist at HSBC Midland, said the figures were disappointing but not a disaster and inflation would fall further in the coming months.
"But the data will make another early rate cut a risky exerecise for Mr Clarke," he said.
Economists said price trends in the coming months could hinge on whether the country's hard-pressed retailers try to mark up their prices and how cost conscious consumers remain.

"The key test of consumers' willingness to pay more will come as summer sales discounts are fully unwound," said David Coleman, economist at CIB Wood Gundy. "This will help to determine if the UK is to remain a low-inflation economy."
